evidence.quote:
A.7 The potential effect of mispricing in the market value of equity

        Because we deflate accruals and cash flows by market value of equity, questions have been

raised about the potential impact of stock mispricing and risk on our results. However, we do not

know of any valid reason why mispricing or risk would result in a strengthening of the association

between accruals and cash flows and the disappearance of the weakening trend in the association

when we deflate by market value of equity. For mispricing or risk to explain our results, not only

would it need to strengthen the association between accruals and cash flows, but its effect would

also need to change over time and result to the disappearance of the weakening trend we

documented. Moreover, prior research suggests that equity market prices are efficient with respect

to the valuation of intangibles (Fama [1998], Barth, Beaver, and Landsman [2001], Aboody and

Lev [1998], Chan, Lakonishok, and Sougiannis [2001], Sougiannis [1994], Lev and Sougiannis

[1996]). Chan et al. [2001, p. 2433], for instance, find that the average stock return for firms with

R&D is comparable to that for firms with no R&D, “consistent with the notion that the market

price on average incorporates fully the benefits of R&D spending.” Nonetheless, we assess the

potential impact of mispricing and risk on our results. First, we use the mispricing score of

Stambaugh, Yu, and Yuan [2015]. 4 This score (MISP) is a rank variable ranging from 1 to 100,

with high value indicating overpricing and low value indicating underpricing. This measure is

proposed to capture the mispricing of a stock by averaging its ranking percentile for each of the

11 anomalies, consisting of net stock issues, composite equity issues, accruals, net operating assets,

asset growth, investment to assets, financial distress, O-score, momentum, gross profitability, and


4
 We thank the authors of Stambaugh et al. [2015] for making their mispricing score publicly available at
http://finance.wharton.upenn.edu/~stambaug/.

                                                         6

return on assets. Second, we use the alpha from the Fama-French three-factor model (Alpha),

consistent with Han et al. [2021]. 5 The alpha is calculated for each firm-year using monthly stock

returns over the 12-month window starting after the fiscal year end month. A stock is deemed

overpriced if its alpha is negative and underpriced otherwise. We note that the mispricing measures

can also capture risk. Finally, we use the standard deviation of monthly stock returns (SDev

Return). Since these measures could be correlated with intangible-intensity (e.g., intangible-

intensive firms are likely to be riskier), We first split firm-years into high and low intangible

subsamples. Then, for each subsample and each of the three measures (i.e., MISP, Alpha, and SDev

Return), we sort firm-years into four quartiles each year. We define Overpriced_MISP

(Underpriced_MISP) as an indicator variable for firm-years in the highest (lowest) mispricing

quartile of MISP. We define Overpriced_Alpha (Underpriced_Alpha) as an indicator variable for

firm-years in the lowest (highest) mispricing quartile of Alpha. Similarly, we define High Risk

(Low Risk) as an indicator variable for firm-years in the highest (lowest) quartile of SDev Return.
evidence.description: Online appendix describes MISP as a 1–100 rank, alpha over 12 months after fiscal year end, and annual quartiles within intangible subsamples.

evidence.quote:
A.8 The accrual-cash flow association with the Dechow and Dichev (2002) model

        Bushman et al. [2016] also study the trend in the association between contemporaneous

accruals and operating cash flows using Dechow and Dichev’s [2002] model, which involves

adding past and future operating cash flows to the right-hand side of the regression. We also

conduct our analysis using the same model. Specifically, we regress accruals on past, current, and



5
 Our results are robust to using the Carhart four-factor model alpha.
6
 The sample size for Column (1) using mispricing score of Stambaugh et al. [2015] is smaller because the data are
available only until 2016.

                                                       7

future cash flows and their interaction terms with a time trend variable (Time). The results, which

we report in Table A8, show that our main inferences are robust to using Dechow and Dichev’s

[2002] model. In particular, we find no evidence of a significantly positive trend in the

contemporaneous association between accruals and cash flows or that the association approaches

zero as documented in Bushman et al. [2016] when we make our adjustments. The coefficient (t-

value) on the interaction between the time trend variable and cash flow is 1.08 (24.70) under the

Bushman et al. [2016] specification, as reported in Column (1) of Table 8. The coefficient (t-value)

falls to −0.13 (−1.43) after we make our numerator and denominator adjustments. Remarkably,

untabulated results show that the overall association (t-value) between the contemporaneous

accruals and cash flows over the entire sample period in the Dechow and Dichev [2002] model

increases from −0.54 (−25.4) under the Bushman et al. [2016] specification to −0.89 (−74.89) after

we apply our numerator and denominator adjustments. The model adjusted R2 also increases from

0.50 to 0.65. In sum, these results strongly indicate that cash flows explain a substantial portion of

the variation in accruals and that our numerator and denominator adjustments substantially

improve the model specification and reduce noise in the variable estimates as firms are getting

more intangible-intensive.
evidence.description: Online appendix describes the Dechow–Dichev robustness analysis with past, current and future operating cash flows.
